newsitem.title: ITALY: Ferre seeks sensuality in shrouding female body.
newsitem.headline: Ferre seeks sensuality in shrouding female body.

text.p: Top Italian designer Gianfranco Ferre said he was seeking to create a new sensuality in covering the female body in his 1997 spring/summer collection on Friday.
Ferre, talking to Reuters backstage before he unveiled the ready-to-wear collection at the Milan shows, dismissed a recent trend of designing underwear to sit outside clothing.
"It's a collection inspired for a very feminine sensual woman without using the common joke of putting underwear outside," the portly, bespectacled designer said.
"It's very sensual because it floats inside the dress. The line is very elongated. The new sensuality is to cover the body," he said.
Ferre dismissed the idea the cutting edge of creativity was in London currently, calling some designs appearing there "impossible-to-wear outfits that would do well in a museum".
"I think fashion needs something different, something that belongs to our lives, something that belongs not just to our culture but our reality," he said.

Milan continued to play an important role in fashion of the 1990s. "I think Milan taught everybody how to build up a certain kind of success, a certain quality, a certain appeal to give to outfits to please everybody in the world," he said.
"The amount that people buy in Italy and sell all over the world is just double of what they buy in other countries."

Ferre, whose seven-year stint as chief designer at Paris fashion house Dior ends this year, said he wanted to develop his business, including into fragrances, but had no plans to launch the firm on the stock market like fashion house Gucci.
"Gucci was a company belonging to just a few people who were not in the end directly involved in the creative section. I want to manage in order to develop the sense of culture that my fashion has."

His collection threw out elegant shadows using narrow column dresses to the ankle without a split and monochrome evening dresses often with a single vertical, opaque panel at the front falling straight from the shoulder.

Colours were crisp white and black, shades of hard or softer pink, and gold and bronze, while transparency featured as a way of lengthening the image, with filmy long sleeves to opaque evening gowns and see-through panels to the lower back, as well as wide black sequinned stripes on filmy black pants.

Evening gowns and trousersuits also included low cut backs with glittering sequinned straps, some coming down in a v-shape like braces over the skin, or visible through a filmy panel cut out of the dress.

For daywear there were pink or white, collared smocktops or outsized shirts hanging comfortably down below the hip at the back, a beige knitted sleeveless dress buttoned down the spine, and plenty of white trousers and matching tailored jackets.
Knits included a series of creamy white tops with collars so wide they fell in folds at angles from naked shoulders.

Earlier, fashion house Fendi produced a collection with a predominantly elongated profile to dresses, starting from the opening cream and black knits decorated with contrasting panels or punctuated at the calf by a wide band of cream below black.

Slip dresses sat over trapeze dresses while tunics draped over ankle length skirts creating "fluid lines emphasised by soft fabrics flowing along the body and then widening into a soft pleat," the fashion house said.
For evening came dresses of black filigree lacquered leaves on tulle, worn with underwear visible beneath, while shoes were high with slender but not spiky heels and slightly raised soles.
The shows move into their penultimate day on Saturday with the major line-up coming from designer Gianni Versace and finishing off with Giorgio Armani's chief collection on Sunday.
